profile.name: Urban Kiz
profile.tagline: A Paris-born partner dance shaping Kizomba roots with hip-hop isolations and linear lines.
profile.insight: Emerging in 2010s Paris, Urban Kiz detached from Kizomba's grounded hips by straightening the legs, tracking geometric lines, and pausing weight transfers through a delayed 'and-principle.'
profile.profile: Urban Kiz is a partner dance created in Paris during the 2010s that diverged from Angolan Kizomba. Pioneered by dancers such as Curtis Seldon, Cherazad Benyoucef, Enah Lebon, and Moun, it took shape against electronic Ghetto-Zouk, Tarraxinha, and hip-hop remixes. Rather than using the grounded body weight and circular patterns of traditional Kizomba, Urban Kiz emphasizes upright frames, straight legs, sharp directional changes at perpendicular angles, and synchronized isolations. After years of circulating online under names like Kizomba 2.0 and French Style, the title 'UrbanKiz' was adopted in 2015 to establish its own identity.
profile.profile_long:
During the 2000s, the Angolan diaspora introduced Kizomba across European hubs, establishing footholds in Portugal, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Spain. In Paris, social media platforms like YouTube and Vimeo accelerated the cross-pollination of this partner dance with other urban genres. By 2008, the dancer Moun was exploring new dynamics on the floor, followed by Curtis Seldon in 2011 and Enah Lebon in 2012. Around 2013, Seldon and Cherazad Benyoucef systematically altered their posture, connection, and dynamics, crystallizing a distinct way of moving.

For several years, this emerging movement lacked a unified definition. Instructors promoted it under transient labels including Kizomba 2.0, French Style Kizomba, New Style Kizomba, and kizomba fusion. The form deliberately departed from Kizomba’s core technique by absorbing elements of hip-hop and Argentine tango, including pivots and pirouettes. Continued friction over its presentation as authentic Kizomba prompted a decisive break; following disputes in 2015, the name UrbanKiz was formally coined and announced to distinguish the style, where 'Urban' reflects Ghetto-Zouk, R&B, and hip-hop musical textures and 'Kiz' acknowledges its ancestral inspiration.

Technically, Urban Kiz replaces the grounded, continuous weight shifting of traditional Kizomba with high body tension, straight legs, and energetic control. Dancers travel across straight tracks, pivoting sharply at perpendicular angles or reversing directions along linear lanes. Movement stops, foot taps, and isolations synchronize tightly with rhythmic hits, drops, and accelerations. A foundational mechanic is the '&-principle', where advancing or retreating feet do not instantly absorb the body's mass; instead, a preliminary tap places merely 10 to 20 percent of the dancer's weight onto the floor before a controlled, gradual transfer takes place.

The dance's sonic foundation centers on dynamic electronic arrangements including Ghetto-Zouk, Tarraxa, Afrobeat, and contemporary remixes featuring rap and dance music. Rather than following an even, cyclical pulse, Urban Kiz musical tracks incorporate sudden breaks, accelerations, and bridge sections that drop down into slow tempos, challenging partners to execute syncopated contratempos. By 2020, Urban Kiz had expanded from Parisian clubs into an international festival circuit spanning Europe and five other continents.

sections.origins_and_history: Urban Kiz developed in Paris during the 2010s as a divergence from Kizomba. During the 2000s, Kizomba was exported abroad and introduced by the Angolan diaspora into countries such as Portugal, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Spain. Early video distribution on YouTube and Vimeo helped popularize alternative approaches. Dancer Moun was active from 2008, Curtis Seldon began in 2011, and Enah Lebon in 2012. In Paris around 2013, Curtis Seldon and Cherazad Benyoucef changed the core movement style. Initially called Kizomba 2.0, French Style Kizomba, New Style Kizomba, or kizomba fusion, the style was officially christened and publicly announced as UrbanKiz in 2015 following disagreements over its relationship to traditional Kizomba.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Urban Kiz is a partner dance characterized by straight legs, upright frames, and higher muscular tension and movement energy compared to grounded Kizomba. Dancers move along straight lines, executing sudden reversals or turning at perpendicular angles. Choreographic mechanics frequently employ hip-hop elements such as stops, taps, and isolations, alongside tango-derived pivots and follower pirouettes. A core technique is the '&-principle', where stepping forward or backward begins with a tap bearing only 10 to 20 percent of body weight before a gradual transfer is completed. Movement timing frequently integrates contratempos synchronized to sudden shifts in the music.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is performed to Ghetto-Zouk, Tarraxinha (Tarraxa), Afrobeat, and remixes featuring R&B, Rap, Dance, and Hip Hop. The music features dynamic shifts in pace, containing bridge transitions to slower tempos, abrupt breaks, and accelerations that dancers match through syncopations and isolations.
sections.costume_and_setting: Originating in social dance scenes and clubs in Paris, Urban Kiz expanded across international dance and music festivals. Specific costuming rules or historical attire are not detailed in the sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Urban Kiz functions as a modern social partner dance. Its development and naming reflected an intentional effort to carve out a distinct identity for dancers blending street dance dynamics with partnered connection, separating it from traditional Angolan Kizomba while maintaining historical lineage.
sections.notable_figures: Key pioneers include Curtis Seldon and Cherazad (Sherazad) Benyoucef, who reshaped the movement around 2013, as well as dancers Enah Lebon and Moun.
sections.regional_variants: The dance originated in Paris, France, and while it remains most prevalent in Europe, by 2020 it spread across dozens of annual festivals across all six developed continents. Local regional variants are not detailed in the sources.
sections.lineage: Urban Kiz directly diverged from Angolan Kizomba, while integrating technical figures and movement concepts from Argentine Tango (such as pivots) as well as body isolations, stops, and taps from Hip Hop.

basic_steps: Establish an upright partner frame with straight legs and body tension
Initiate a forward or backward step using the &-principle by placing a light tap with 10 to 20 percent of body weight
Gradually complete the bodyweight transfer onto the stepping foot
Travel along a straight linear path rather than circular curves
Change direction sharply at a perpendicular angle or reverse along the line
Perform stops, foot taps, and upper-body isolations matching musical breaks
Execute pivots or pirouettes for the follower during open or linear transitions
teaching.rhythm: Dynamic and variable tempo with breaks, accelerations, and contratempos matching Ghetto-Zouk and hip-hop beats
teaching.formation: Two-person partner dance moving along straight linear lanes
teaching.level_notes: Beginners must master the '&-principle' of delayed weight transfers, maintain straight-leg tension, and navigate perpendicular angles without defaulting to grounded circular hip motion.

gaps: No specific musical albums or single track titles are documented in the source text.
Costuming conventions and traditional dress guidelines are absent from the provided material.

claims.text: Urban Kiz is a partner dance and music genre that originated in Paris during the 2010s.
claims.quote: Urbankiz (or UrbanKiz) is a partner dance and music genre that developed in Paris during the 2010s.

claims.text: The dance evolved from Kizomba and blends styles such as Ghetto-Zouk, Tarraxinha, Afrobeat, and hip-hop remixes.
claims.quote: The dance diverged from Kizomba and incorporates various music styles such as Ghetto-Zouk, Tarraxinha, Afrobeat and remixes with R&B, Rap and Hip Hop.

claims.text: Curtis Seldon and Cherazad Benyoucef created the dance in Paris around 2013 by altering the movement style.
claims.quote: UrbanKiz was created in Paris somewhere during 2013. by Curtis Seldon and Cherazad (also spelled Sherazad) Benyoucef who were the first to change the way to dance.

claims.text: The dance was widely pioneered in Paris by Curtis Seldon, Enah Lebon, and Moun.
claims.quote: it's widely accepted that the brand UrbanKiz was pioneered in Paris by famous dancers Curtis Seldon, Enah Lebon and Moun.

claims.text: Before settling on a final name, the dance was referred to as Kizomba 2.0, French Style Kizomba, New Style Kizomba, and kizomba fusion.
claims.quote: The dance still went under various names, such as Kizomba 2.0, French Style Kizomba, New Style Kizomba, kizomba fusion, because no consensus was reached on a final name.

claims.text: The name UrbanKiz was formally announced and adopted in 2015 after disputes over its separation from Kizomba.
claims.quote: After fights in 2015 the new name UrbanKiz was created and publicly announced.

claims.text: Urban Kiz features straight legs and elevated tension compared to the grounded body posture of Kizomba.
claims.quote: Furthermore, while in Kizomba, the dance is more grounded, in Urban Kiz, the legs are straight and the body has more tension and movement energy.

claims.text: Urban Kiz patterns travel in straight lines or change at perpendicular angles or direction reversals.
claims.quote: The figures often require movement along straight lines or changing direction only at perpendicular angles or reversing direction.

claims.text: The &-principle involves a preliminary foot tap carrying 10 to 20 percent of weight followed by a gradual weight transfer.
claims.quote: The &-principle means that a step forward or backward does not directly lead to a shift of body weight, but it first starts with a tap of the moving foot (10-20% of body weight on that foot) and is followed by a gradual bodyweight transfer to that foot.

claims.text: Urban Kiz incorporates elements from Hip Hop like stops, taps, and isolations, as well as tango pivots and follower pirouettes.
claims.quote: Urban kiz dancers synchronize their body movement to the music by using elements that are also present in Hip Hop, such as stops, taps, and isolations.

claims.text: As of 2020, Urban Kiz is featured annually in dozens of dance and music festivals across six continents.
claims.quote: As of 2020 Urban Kiz is danced in many countries, and still spreading fast all over the world. Though the dance and culture are still most prevalent in Europe, Urban Kiz is featured annually in dozens of dance and music festivals across all six developed continents.
